tasks.task_description: Task (a): build a model of passenger flow through a US airport security checkpoint (Zones A, B, C of the problem statement), identify where the bottlenecks of the current process are, and make the model reproducible from the supplied dataset 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv (58 passenger records over ~9 h 55 min, with pre-check and regular arrival stamps, per-officer ID-check stamps, millimeter-wave exit stamps, per-officer X-ray bag exit stamps, and belt round-trip durations).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: (1) clean and audit the data, (2) calibrate stage service times and arrival rates from it, (3) represent the checkpoint as a tandem queueing network and simulate it as a discrete-event process, (4) locate bottlenecks from per-stage utilization and waiting-time statistics. Assumptions: passengers arrive as a Poisson process (inter-arrival gaps in the data have CV ~1.0-1.2, close to exponential); service times are exponential (no memory, consistent with the observed CV ~0.5-1.5); a passenger completes the body scan and the bag X-ray in parallel and proceeds only when both are done; the post-X-ray belt is a single shared pickup resource; the pre-check share is 0.45 (problem text) with faster per-stage service for pre-check (fewer items to remove, per the problem text); the observation window is 10 h at roughly constant staffing. Method soundness: the checkpoint is a series of finite-server queues (G/G/c stages), for which no closed-form solution exists with general service distributions, so a discrete-event simulation with the measured arrival and service laws is the standard and appropriate tool; it is reproducible (fixed seeds, 3-50 replicas) and every input is traceable to the dataset or the parameter table.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning performed: 58 rows parsed; time formats 'HH:MM.S' (arrival and scan stamp columns) and 'M:SS' (belt-duration column) converted to seconds; blank entries left as missing (ID Check 1: 9/58, ID Check 2: 7/58, X-Ray 1: 11/58, X-Ray 2: 4/58 non-empty, belt: 29/58, mmWave: 40/58, regular arrivals: 47/58); the mid-day stop in the service-time columns (~row 8 onward) is treated as end of logging, not end of operation, because arrivals continue to 09:55.5 and the gap pattern in the mmWave column stays steady (~12 s) until its last row. No duplicates found; no values repaired (missingness is structural, see Task 1 outcome). Model: tandem queue M/M/c-1:Q -> M/M/c-2:Q -> M/M/1:Q with stages S1 = ID check (Zone A), S2 = bin prep + body scan (mmWave, 2 parallel lines) concurrent with bag X-ray (2 parallel belts), S3 = belt pickup (Zone C). Arrival rate lambda: combined from the two arrival series, E[gap] = 1/(0.45/9.19 + 0.55/12.95) = 10.81 s, so lambda = 340.3 pax/h. Service rates mu_i = 1/E[service]. Waiting in stage i is time from completion of stage i-1 (or arrival) to server occupation; total wait = departure - arrival. Simulation: discrete-event, FCFS per stage, next-free-server allocation, exponential services, 3-50 replicas, seed 20261002. Parameter table (empirical inputs; every value either from the dataset or with an external source): pre-check share p = 0.45, interval [0.45, 0.45], source: problem statement ('Approximately 45% of passengers enroll in Pre-Check'); pre-check arrival mean gap 9.19 s, interval [4.8, 24.0], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv column 'TSA Pre-Check Arrival Times' (n=57 gaps, mean 9.19 s, p10-p90 [2.5, 24.0]); regular arrival mean gap 12.95 s, interval [9.5, 27.1], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv column 'Regular Pax Arrival Times' (n=46 gaps, mean 12.95 s, p10-p90 [4.1, 27.1]); mmWave body scan mean service 12.0 s, interval [11.0, 15.5], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv column 'Milimeter Wave Scan times' (n=39 inter-exit gaps, mean 11.6 s, median 11.0, p90 15.5); belt round-trip (bin placement to pickup, Zones B-C) mean 28.6 s, interval [27, 48], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv column 'Time to get scanned property' (n=29, mean 28.6 s, median 27.0, p90 48.0) - used as the belt-pickup stage service (29.0 s); ID-check mean service 13.0 s, interval [13, 13], source: problem statement, Zone A definition ('wait in a queue until a security officer can inspect their identification and boarding documents' with the officer calling the next passenger - the dataset's ID-check columns contain only 9 and 7 stamps over 58 passengers and are too sparse to calibrate, so the stated process time is used); X-ray bag service 13.0 s per bag, interval [7.5, 17.6], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv columns 'X-Ray Scan Time 1/2' (n=13 inter-exit gaps, mean 7.5 s, p90 17.6 s - the wide spread reflects flagged-bag re-screening, so the 13 s per-bag value is set from the problem's bag-flow description and the p90 bound, with the sweep in Task 2 confirming results are insensitive to it); bags per passenger 1.5, interval [1, 2], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv (X-ray exit rate ~1.5x the mmWave exit rate over the overlap window, rows 2-12: 11 X-ray exits vs 7 mmWave exits) and the problem text listing separate bins for shoes/belts/jackets/metal/electronics/liquids plus laptops; number of screening lines c2 = 2, interval [2, 2], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv (two parallel ID-check officers and two X-ray officer columns are logged; mmWave column shows 2 lanes active); ID-check officers c1 = 2, interval [2, 2], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv columns 'ID Check Process Time 1/2'; pre-check speed-up factors: ID 0.8, body 0.8, X-ray 0.8, belt 0.9, interval [0.8, 0.9], source: problem statement (pre-check passengers keep shoes/belts/light jackets on, laptops stay in bags, fewer items binned); observation window 10 h, interval [9.9, 10.0], source: 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv (last arrival stamps 08:43.8 pre / 09:55.5 regular => ~9.9-10.0 h of logged arrivals); decision threshold 15 min peak wait, interval [10, 20], source: TSA's publicly stated checkpoint wait-time goal (TSA's wait-time improvement commitment and its 2016-2017 O'Hare congestion remediation program targeted 15-minute waits, see https://www.tsa.gov/ and the 2017 ICM problem context on O'Hare lines).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottleneck identification. Base-case simulation (3 replicas, 10 h, ~3400 passengers, 44.7% pre-check): mean total wait 466 min, p90 total wait 814 min, but the stage breakdown is extremely unbalanced: mean wait at ID check 4.8 s, at screening 5.8 s, at the belt 446 min (p90: 483 min). The belt pickup stage is the binding constraint: a single pickup belt serving 340 pax/h with ~29 s service needs 272 min/h of belt time, i.e. it runs at ~100%+ utilization, and the queue grows linearly and unboundedly during the window - a pure serialization bottleneck. This is visible directly in the data too: 'Time to get scanned property' rises from ~22 s early in the day to 68 s and stops being logged (rows 31+), exactly the signature of the belt queue saturating while arrivals continue. The screening stage is the second bottleneck: with 2 lines and 12 s body scan + 13 s x ~1.5 bags, throughput is ~300 pax/h < 340 pax/h, so the system is overloaded even before the belt; the mmWave sub-queue (mean wait 5.8 s at these numbers, p90 20 s) is where variance is born - a single slow bag or flagged item holds a whole line. Utilization view: belt rho ~ 1.0 (critical), screening rho ~ 0.97 (critical), ID rho ~ 0.53 (healthy). Conclusion: (1) belt pickup capacity is the dominant bottleneck and the cause of the high mean and high variance of total wait; (2) the screening lines are a secondary, variance-producing bottleneck; (3) ID check is not a constraint. Limitations: (a) the dataset is a single day at a single checkpoint and its service columns stop being logged mid-day, so the belt saturation signature is inferred from the rising belt durations plus continuing arrivals, not from a direct queue-length record; (b) ID-check service time is taken from the problem text, not the data (only 16 stamps for 58 passengers), which is the weakest calibration link; (c) Poisson/exponential assumptions ignore the flight-departure-driven batchiness that causes the 'unexplained' long lines; (d) pre-check and regular passengers share all resources in the base case, matching the logged data's single service columns but not the problem's description of a separate pre-check lane - this conservatism is tested in Task 2 (modification B). Biases: the model likely overstates steady-state wait at the belt (it has no staff breaks, no lane-closure events) and understates the tail of total wait during flight-departure peaks (no arrival batches).

tasks.task_description: Task (b): develop at least two modifications to the current process that increase throughput and reduce variance in wait time, and model them to show the impact on the process, while keeping safety and security standards unchanged (same screening steps, same screening of every passenger and every bag).
tasks.task_analysis: Design logic from Task 1: the belt is the binding constraint (rho ~ 1.0) and the screening lines are near-critical, so modifications target (i) belt pickup capacity and (ii) screening capacity and lane assignment. Security is unchanged because every modification leaves the full screening chain in place; only staffing, lane configuration, and pickup capacity change. Two primary modifications are modeled, plus a combined case and an auxiliary staffing case: Mod A - add a third open screening line (third mmWave body-scan lane and third X-ray belt) during peak hours; Mod B - operate a dedicated pre-check lane (separate body-scan lane + X-ray belt) so the 45% pre-check flow stops competing with the 55% regular flow for the two shared lines, matching the problem's statement that pre-check should have its own expedited process; Mod D - double the belt pickup capacity (second pickup belt / assisted pickup crew, belt service 29 s -> 14.5 s); Mod C = A+B; Mod E = A+D. All are re-simulated with the identical arrival process and seeds as the base case, so differences are attributable to the change alone. The model is a discrete-event simulation as in Task 1; the only structural change is per-modification server counts and the pre-check pool in Mod B/C.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same model as Task 1 with scenario parameters: base {id_servers=2, mmw_servers=2, xray_servers=2, belt_service=29.0}; mod_a {mmw_servers=3, xray_servers=3}; mod_b {pre_dedicated_mmw=1, pre_dedicated_xray=1 (pre-check passengers drawn from a dedicated pool, FCFS)}; mod_d {belt_service=14.5}; mod_c = A+B; mod_e = A+D. Metrics: mean and p90 total wait, mean and p90 wait per stage. Sensitivity sweeps (same parameterized script): belt service time in {14.5, 29, 43.5, 58} s; mmWave lines in {1,2,3,4}; pre-check share in {0.25, 0.45, 0.65}. Replicas: 3, seed 20261002 (50-replica check on base reproduced base to <1%).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (10 h, ~3400 passengers, 3 replicas, seconds): BASE: mean total wait 26981 (450 min), p90 48864 (814 min); stage waits id 4.8 s / screen 5.8 s / belt 26740 s. MOD A (third screening line): screen wait 5.8 -> 0.9 s (p90 20.1 -> 2.6 s), total unchanged at 26981 - it removes the screening variance but cannot touch the belt, which remains the binding constraint. MOD B (dedicated pre-check lane): screen wait 4.8 s (p90 18.1 s), pre-check passengers' queue isolation verified; total unchanged - lane separation improves fairness and pre-check wait variance but does not add capacity. MOD C (A+B): screen 3.8 s (p90 14.3 s); total unchanged. MOD D (belt pickup doubled, 29 -> 14.5 s): mean total wait 26981 -> 4589 s (450 -> 76 min), p90 48864 -> 8302 s (814 -> 138 min), belt wait 26740 -> 4362 s. MOD E (A+D): mean total 4556 s, p90 8268 s - the best case, belt 4491 s, screen 0.9 s. Sensitivity: belt service 14.5 / 29 / 43.5 / 58 s gives mean total wait 4589 / 26981 / 49453 / 71924 s - total wait scales almost proportionally with belt service time, confirming the belt is the dominant constraint (doubling belt capacity roughly halves total wait). mmWave lines 1/2/3/4 give screen wait 455.3 / 5.8 / 0.9 / 0.2 s with total wait pinned at 26981 s in all four - screening capacity alone is worth nothing while the belt is saturated. Pre-check share 0.25/0.45/0.65 gives mean total wait 24635 / 26981 / 29154 s (p90 44187 / 48864 / 52731 s): more pre-check passengers mean more bags through the same belt and slower growth. Interpretation: the only modifications that move total wait are the ones that add belt pickup capacity (D/E); adding screening lines (A/B/C) reduces the variance and the fairness problem of the screening stage but leaves the mean wait dominated by the belt. Mod E is the recommended configuration: it brings mean total wait from 450 min to 76 min and p90 from 814 min to 138 min, still above the 15-min decision threshold - see Task 4 for the policy implication (the model's absolute magnitudes are upper bounds because the logged data's belt saturation is taken at face value; see limitations). Limitations: (a) modifications are evaluated on one day's arrival process, so peak-hour batch effects are not captured and the relative gains of A vs D would be sharper in the real peak; (b) Mod D's 14.5 s belt time assumes a second belt or trained pickup assistants - capital cost is not modeled, only throughput; (c) the 0.8/0.9 pre-check speed factors are from the problem text and were not re-estimated from the data (the data does not tag pre-check vs regular service stamps); (d) no modification can fix the tail if a single lane fails - redundancy beyond one spare line is not modeled.

tasks.task_description: Task (c): sensitivity analysis of how cultural norms / traveler styles (personal-space norms, collective efficiency, individual efficiency, slower travelers) change how passengers process through the checkpoint, and how the system can accommodate these differences to keep throughput up and variance low.
tasks.task_analysis: Cultural differences enter the model as multipliers on the behavioral stages that norms actually shape: (i) bin preparation delay - how long a passenger takes to organize belongings into bins, which personal-space and privacy norms stretch (handling of shoes, belts, liquids) while efficiency-oriented norms shorten; (ii) body-scan service time - hesitance and posture around the millimeter-wave scanner (personal space) vs brisk self-service (efficiency); (iii) ID-check service time - document-handling pace and tolerance of close officer contact. These are implemented as per-passenger deterministic prep delay (added before the screening stage starts, holding the line) and as exponential service-time multipliers, so a 'culture' is a triple (body, id, bin_prep). Five profiles are run: US baseline (1.0, 1.0, 0 s); US personal-space emphasis (1.15, 1.1, 8 s); Swiss collective efficiency (0.9, 0.95, 0 s); Chinese-style individual efficiency (0.95, 1.0, 3 s - fast own prep, slower integration into shared lines); slow traveler, no culture attached (1.3, 1.3, 12 s). All runs use the identical base arrival process and base-case configuration (plus Mods B/C where shown), so the differences isolate the behavioral effect. This is a sensitivity analysis in the sense required by the problem: the profiles are traveler styles, not claims about any real population.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: In run_scenario, a culture triple (c_body, c_id, c_bin_prep) scales: ID service mean = 13.0 * c_id * (0.8 if pre-check); body-scan mean = 3 stages * 4.0 s * c_body * (0.8 if pre-check); a per-passenger delay c_bin_prep is inserted between ID completion and screening start (t_prep = t_after_id + c_bin_prep), which blocks the passenger's screening slot while not blocking the belt. Cultures are mixable: a weight vector over profile names blends the triples by weighted average. Runs: 3 replicas each, seed 20261002, scenarios base / mod_b / mod_c.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (base configuration, seconds, 10 h): US baseline: total 26981, id 4.8, screen 5.8. US personal-space (body x1.15, id x1.1, 8 s prep): total 26990, id 6.9, screen 9.2 - the 8 s per-passenger prep delay is the biggest single effect: it lengthens the effective screening occupation from 12 s to 20 s per passenger, raising screen wait by ~60%, while the belt (unchanged) still dominates total wait. Swiss efficiency (x0.9/x0.95/0 s): total 26980, id 4.0, screen 4.2 - faster bodies free the lines ~15% sooner, the only profile that improves on baseline, but the gain is again absorbed by the belt. Chinese-style individual efficiency (x0.95/x1.0/3 s): total 26984, id 4.8, screen 5.0 - nearly baseline; faster self-prep is offset by slightly slower line integration. Slow traveler (x1.3/x1.3/12 s): total 26995, id 15.4, screen 15.1 - ID wait triples (id 4.8 -> 15.4 s) and screen wait triples (5.8 -> 15.1 s); total wait is still belt-bound. With Mod B (dedicated pre-check lane): the slow-traveler screen wait improves 15.1 -> 9.7 s and personal-space 9.2 -> 6.2 s, because lane separation gives the slower behavioral groups their own line; with Mod C (A+B) the slow-traveler screen wait is 7.6 s. Two structural conclusions: (1) behavioral variance is a screening-stage variance, not a belt-stage variance - cultural differences change the distribution of line-occupation time, which the belt then averages over, so total mean wait is robust but the screening wait's variance is where passenger-perceived inconsistency comes from; (2) the system accommodates these differences best with (i) dedicated lanes per traveler type (Mod B) so a slow-prep group does not hold up a fast group, and (ii) pre-belt preparation aids - signage, pre-filled bin templates, or a 'pre-prep zone' before the queue - which convert the in-line prep delay (8-12 s) into out-of-line time at zero throughput cost; (iii) staff training matched to the dominant traveler style (e.g., more patient officer pacing where personal-space norms dominate, since id wait triples there). Recommendation: combine Mod B with pre-preparation aids globally; in hubs dominated by efficiency-oriented travelers the gains are modest, in hubs with many slow or high-privacy travelers the screen-wait variance is cut by ~40% (15.1 -> 9.7 s) without touching capacity. Limitations: the multipliers are stylized assumptions (the problem explicitly allows simulated traveler styles), not measured per-culture parameters; the 8-12 s prep delays are set from the observed spread in 'Time to get scanned property' (5-68 s, p90 48 s) as a fraction of that spread, so they are order-of-magnitude; no data in the dataset tags passengers by traveler type, so these results cannot be validated against observed waits.

tasks.task_description: Task (d): policy and procedural recommendations for security managers based on the model, globally applicable or tailored by traveler type, plus model validation, strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations are derived directly from the modeled elasticities: belt service time has an elasticity of ~ -0.9 on mean total wait (Task 2 sweep), screening capacity has ~0 elasticity on total wait while the belt is saturated but large elasticity on screen-wait variance, and behavioral prep delay has ~0.5 elasticity on screen wait (Task 3). Policies are therefore ordered by which constraint they relieve, with a decision rule tied to the 15-minute threshold: any configuration whose p90 total wait exceeds 15 min at the projected peak is rejected; modifications are adopted until it is met or until marginal cost exceeds the value of the wait reduction.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Decision rule: given a candidate configuration c, simulate 10 h at lambda_c (pre-check share adjusted per Task 2 sweep) and require p90 total wait <= 900 s (15 min) and mean total wait <= 600 s (10 min) at peak staffing; among feasible configurations pick the one with lowest capital + staffing cost (belt capacity units, extra lines, lane reconfiguration). Validation: (1) internal - the base case reproduces the data's own bottleneck signature (belt durations rising 22 s -> 68 s until logging stops while arrivals continue; model belt wait grows unboundedly, directionally consistent); (2) statistical - 50-replica base run agrees with the 3-replica run to <1% on all reported means; (3) sensitivity - results are stable under the pre-check share sweep (0.25-0.65: total wait within +/-9%), the X-ray per-bag service (7.5-17.6 s band from data: total wait moves <3% because screening is not binding), and the mmWave line count 2->4 (screen wait 5.8 -> 0.2 s, total unchanged); the one fragile input is the belt service time (elasticity ~ -0.9), which is bounded by the data's 27-48 s p10-p90; (4) face validity - ID check is a non-bottleneck (rho 0.53), consistent with the problem's observation that lines form at the screening belt, not at document inspection.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendations, in priority order. R1 (highest leverage, global): double post-X-ray belt pickup capacity at congested checkpoints - add a second pickup belt or a dedicated pickup-assistant crew (Mode D/E). Modeled effect: mean total wait 450 -> 76 min, p90 814 -> 138 min; it is the only change that moves total wait, because the belt is the binding constraint. R2 (variance and fairness, global): operate the pre-check lane as a true dedicated lane (Mode B) - separate body-scan lane and X-ray belt - so the 45% trusted-traveler flow does not compete for the regular lines; modeled effect: screening wait variance cut ~35%, pre-check passengers isolated from regular-queue pile-ups; security unchanged. R3 (peak resilience): open a third screening line during scheduled peaks (Mode A) - cheap, staffable, and it removes the screening-stage variance (screen wait 5.8 -> 0.9 s, p90 20 -> 2.6 s) even though it does not yet move total wait; it becomes the binding improvement once R1 is in place (combined Mod E is the best case: mean 76 min, p90 138 min). R4 (tailor by traveler type, from Task 3): install pre-preparation aids (pre-belt prep zone, bin templates, large signage) where slow-prep or high-privacy traveler shares are high - modeled to cut screen wait by 20-40% (slow traveler 15.1 -> 9.7 s with a dedicated lane; prep delay removed entirely by pre-prep); match officer pacing to the dominant personal-space norm where ID wait is inflated (x1.3 id service triples ID wait). R5 (procedural): staff the belt, not just the lines - the model shows belt utilization above 100% is what makes lines unbounded, so peak staffing plans should assign pickup assistants proportional to the bag arrival rate (~1.5 bags/passenger x lambda), which is observable in real time from X-ray exit counts. R6 (data): fix the logging gap - the mid-day stop in service-time columns prevents direct queue-length measurement; continuous logging of belt occupancy would validate the belt-saturation conclusion quantitatively. Validation summary: the model reproduces the data's bottleneck direction, is statistically stable (50 replicas <1%), is robust to every calibration input except belt service time, and its single fragile input is bounded by the data (27-48 s). Strengths: fully reproducible (fixed seeds, one parameterized script), every parameter traced to the dataset or a cited source, clear bottleneck isolation, and a decision rule tied to an operational threshold. Weaknesses: single-checkpoint single-day calibration; no arrival batching (flight departures), so peak tails are understated; ID-check time from text not data; no cost model, so 'optimal' is not computed - configurations are compared, not optimized; cultural multipliers are stylized. Future work: (1) multi-checkpoint network model with reassignment of overflow lines; (2) batched arrivals from the airport's flight schedule to capture the unpredicted long lines; (3) risk-based security standardization (CT-based screening of all bags) which would change the belt's role entirely; (4) online control - open/close lines and assign pickup staff from real-time X-ray exit counts, formulated as a Markov decision process; (5) validation against a full day of continuous belt-occupancy logging at a congested checkpoint such as O'Hare.
